**Subject: The building on rue Saint-Hubert — stop the sale and call me**

Denis,

I am writing this down because I am too angry to trust myself to say everything clearly on the phone. I want you to read this properly and understand exactly what you have done and what it means to me.

I am furious. Not just disappointed, not just hurt. Furious.

You are putting Papa’s building on the market behind my back — the building where my bakery has been for 31 years. And I did not learn it from you. I learned it from a stranger with a camera who walked into my shop at six o’clock on Thursday morning, while I was shaping the baguettes.

A photographer from the agency came into my bakery and told me that Mr. Denis had said I was okay with it. I was not okay with it. I did not even know there was a listing. I was standing in my own shop, doing my work, and suddenly there was a man with a camera behaving as if everything had already been arranged. Karine had to calm me down. Afterward, I went online and found the building on Centris myself, listed with an agent for $1,150,000.

Can you imagine what that felt like? My own brother could not call me, but an agency could send somebody into my bakery before sunrise.

You did not even have the decency to tell me yourself. You used an agent and left a photographer to break the news to me. That was avoiding me, and it was deeply disrespectful.

After Maman’s funeral, you called me and said, “No rush, we decide together.”

Together, Denis. That was the word you used.

There was nothing together about this. You made a decision that affects my business, my income, my employees and the rest of my working life, and you did it without even giving me the respect of a conversation. Did you think I would simply accept it once it was already online? Did you think I would calm down and let the agent handle me too?

Papa bought that three-storey building on rue Saint-Hubert in 1979. The bakery is on the ground floor, with the two apartments above. Since Maman died in February and the estate was settled in August, it has belonged half to you and half to me. I have paid $2,400 a month in rent to the estate and have never once been late. In 2019, I paid $38,000 myself for the new roof. I did that because this is not some temporary shop to me. I have been maintaining my workplace and investing in a building that was also my family’s.

My lease runs until April 30, 2027. You know that. You also know that I have six employees. This is not only about my feelings or about being attached to old memories. There are six jobs connected to that bakery. There are 31 years of customers who come through that door. There is the work I do every morning before most people are awake. You may think I am being sentimental, but even if you take the sentiment completely out of it, it is still a business and a livelihood.

If a developer buys the building, tears it down, turns it into condos or doubles my rent, my bakery cannot survive that. I cannot simply pick up 31 years of business and move it somewhere else as if it were a sign on a wall. You are not just selling bricks and land from where you sit in Calgary. You are putting everything I have built at risk.

And the worst part is that you did this after I had already told you I wanted to buy your half.

I told you by phone in September that the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. I know that buying your half requires a serious discussion about price, financing and the rest of the numbers. I am not pretending that one pre-approval settles everything. But it was a serious starting point, and you knew I was prepared to pursue it. Instead of discussing it with me, you listed the whole building for $1,150,000 and left me to discover it in the most humiliating way possible.

You may have decided that it is easier to deal with an agent than with your own family. Perhaps it is easier for you. It is not easier for me. You have put me in a position where I have to defend my bakery against my own brother.

So I will be very clear about what I want.

I want the building taken off the market this week. Stop the visits, the photographs and the marketing. Do not take further steps toward a sale while leaving me outside the discussion. I am not asking you to “think about it” while everything continues quietly in the background until I calm down. I am asking you to stop.

At the very least, I want the first opportunity to buy your half, with a real chance to put together and discuss a complete purchase proposal before you accept or pursue an outside offer. I am not asking you to give me your share or to treat me unfairly in business. I am asking you to deal with me directly and seriously instead of selling my workplace out from under me without warning.

And I want your answer from you, by telephone. Not a text from your wife. Not a message passed through the agent. You call me yourself. We may both be angry during that conversation, but at least it will be honest, and at least it will finally be between the two of us.

I also want to say something about Papa’s building that has nothing to do with listings, prices or financing. When we were children, Papa used to let you sleep in the little room at the back where the flour sacks were kept. You loved it. You have your own memories there too. That building is not something only I imagine when I talk about our family. You were there. You know what it was like.

I am not bringing that up because I expect a building to remain frozen in time forever. I am bringing it up because I cannot understand how you could treat this as something so routine that an agency could handle it without you even speaking to me first.

I am not writing this letter because I hate you. I do not hate you. You are still my brother, and I do not want this to be the thing that destroys our relationship. But you need to understand that what you have done has already damaged my trust in you. Loving you does not mean I will accept being treated this way, and it does not mean I will stay quiet to keep the peace.

I am more angry with you than I know how to express properly. I am also asking you, clearly and directly, to make this right before it goes any further.

Take the building off the market. Give me the chance to buy your half. Then pick up the phone and talk to me yourself.

I do not want to lose my brother. But I will not quietly lose my bakery either.

Call me.

[Your name]
